summary: Defines protocol and deployment requirements for the DNS root name service, a critical part of Internet architecture. Operational requirements are out of scope.

plainLanguage.summary: The DNS root is the first place the Internet's directory of names is consulted. This document lists what the root servers must be able to do: speak standard DNS, carry queries over IPv4 and IPv6 and over UDP and TCP, check UDP checksums, implement DNSSEC, and implement the DNS extension mechanisms.

subtitle: The short list of protocol and deployment rules that every DNS root name service must follow.

tldr.problem: The DNS root name service is the top of the Internet's directory of names, and RFC 2870 mixed protocol rules with day-to-day operating rules that had both drifted since it was published.
tldr.mechanism: This document keeps only the protocol rules and a small number of deployment rules, each written as a MUST requirement: core DNS, IPv4 and IPv6, UDP and TCP, UDP checksums, DNSSEC and EDNS(0).
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2870. The operational rules moved to RSSAC-001, and the two documents together replace RFC 2870.

today: RFC 7720 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 40) published in December 2015. It obsoletes RFC 2870, and with RSSAC-001 it functionally replaces that document. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Root Name Service Is
sections.content:
The DNS root name service is the top level of the Domain Name System (DNS), the directory that maps names to addresses. The root servers are the authoritative servers for the unique root zone, written ".". They currently also serve the root-servers.net zone, and some of them also serve the zone for the .arpa top-level domain.

This document describes the external interface of the root name servers from the protocol point of view of the service. It specifies basic requirements for the Internet, meaning what DNS clients can expect when they interact with a root name service over the public Internet. It uses the RFC 2119 keywords such as MUST and SHOULD to say how strong each requirement is.
sections.plainLanguage: The root servers are the top of the Internet's phone book. This document says what a client can count on when it asks them a question.

sections.title: Why RFC 2870 Was Split
sections.content:
RFC 2870 discussed both the protocol requirements and the operational requirements for root name servers. Since it was published, both sets of requirements evolved, so the authors found it made more sense to separate the two sets into two separate documents.

This document defines only the protocol requirements and some deployment requirements. The operational requirements that were defined in RFC 2870 were removed; they are now defined by the Root Server System Advisory Committee (RSSAC) of ICANN and documented in RSSAC-001. RFC 7720 obsoletes RFC 2870, and these two documents together functionally replace it.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook mixed technical rules with running rules, and both had moved on. So the rules were split in two: this document keeps the technical ones, and another group publishes the day-to-day ones.

sections.title: Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
These are the minimum high-level protocol requirements. The operative details are documented in RSSAC-001. The root name service:

  • MUST implement core DNS and the clarifications to the DNS;
  • MUST support IPv4 and IPv6 transport of DNS queries and responses;
  • MUST support UDP and TCP transport of DNS queries and responses;
  • MUST generate checksums when sending UDP datagrams, and MUST verify checksums when receiving UDP datagrams containing a non-zero checksum;
  • MUST implement DNSSEC as an authoritative name service;
  • MUST implement the extension mechanisms for DNS, EDNS(0).
sections.plainLanguage: Every root server has to speak ordinary DNS, work over both old and new Internet addresses and over both packet and connection protocols, and support the two extensions that DNS grew later: the security extension and the extension mechanism.

sections.title: Deployment Requirements
sections.content:
Two deployment rules apply to the root name service. It MUST answer queries from any entity conforming to RFC 1122 with a valid IP address. It also MUST serve the unique root zone.

The effect of the first rule is that a client that behaves properly, wherever it sits on the Internet, gets an answer. The effect of the second is that every root server hands out the same single root zone, rather than a private alternative of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The root servers must answer any client that asks correctly, and they must all serve the same one official list of names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document does not specify a new protocol. It does note that the root name service is a key component of the Internet architecture and plays a key role in the overall security of the Internet.

The security considerations for the DNS protocols themselves are discussed in their respective specifications. The security considerations on the operational side of the root name servers are discussed in RSSAC-001.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is defined here, so there is no new risk either. The detailed safety rules live in the DNS specifications and in the document about running the root servers.

sections.title: The Specifications It Relies On
sections.content:
The document leans on several earlier specifications. Core DNS is defined in RFC 1035, with clarifications in RFC 2181. Transport comes from RFC 791 for IPv4, RFC 2460 for IPv6, RFC 768 for UDP and RFC 793 for TCP. DNSSEC comes from RFC 4035 and the extension mechanisms, EDNS(0), come from RFC 6891. RFC 1122 defines what a conforming host is, and RFC 2826 is the IAB Technical Comment on the Unique DNS Root.

Two references are not RFCs: RSSAC-001, the Root Server System Advisory Committee's Service Expectations of Root Servers from November 2014, and the Root Zone file itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule points back to the specification it comes from, so an implementer can read the DNS rules, the transport rules and the security rules in their own documents.
